title: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
author: Stephen R. Covey
tagline: A principle-centred path from dependence to independence to interdependence.

superpower.name: Principle-Centred Leader
superpower.description: You act from values, not moods.

overview: Covey argues that real effectiveness comes from character and timeless principles rather than quick techniques. The first three habits build personal independence (the private victory), the next three build effective relationships (the public victory), and the seventh keeps all of them renewed.

chapters.title: Inside-Out
chapters.summary: Covey contrasts the 'personality ethic' — techniques and image — with the 'character ethic' of integrity, humility and fairness. Our paradigms, the maps through which we see the world, shape our behaviour, so lasting change comes from shifting how we see things. Change starts inside-out: with ourselves before others.
keyIdeas: Paradigms shape what we see and do.
chapters.tryThis: Notice one situation where changing how you see it would change how you act.

quiz.question: What does Covey say real effectiveness rests on?
quiz.explanation: The character ethic, not the personality ethic.

chapters.title: The Seven Habits — An Overview
chapters.summary: A habit sits where knowledge (what and why), skill (how) and desire (want to) meet. The habits move us along a maturity continuum from dependence (you take care of me) to independence (I can do it) to interdependence (we can do it better together). Effectiveness balances production with protecting our capacity to produce — the 'P/PC balance', like the goose and the golden egg.
keyIdeas: Balance results with the capacity to produce them.
chapters.tryThis: Identify one 'golden goose' in your life that you're overworking.

quiz.question: What three elements make a habit?
quiz.explanation: All three must be present for a habit to form.

chapters.title: Habit 1: Be Proactive
chapters.summary: Between what happens to us and how we respond is a space where we choose. Proactive people take responsibility ('response-ability') and focus on their Circle of Influence — things they can act on — instead of their Circle of Concern. Reactive language ('I have to', 'they make me') hands our power away.
keyIdeas: Focus on your Circle of Influence.
chapters.tryThis: Replace 'I have to' with 'I choose to' for one day.

quiz.question: Where do proactive people focus their energy?
quiz.explanation: Acting where you can make a difference grows your influence.

chapters.title: Habit 2: Begin with the End in Mind
chapters.summary: All things are created twice: first in the mind, then in reality. Covey invites you to picture your own funeral and what you'd want people to say, then write a personal mission statement rooted in principles. With a clear destination, you can judge each day's choices against what truly matters.
chapters.tryThis: Write three sentences on how you'd like to be remembered.

quiz.question: What tool does Habit 2 recommend?
quiz.explanation: It defines the 'end' you're working toward.

chapters.title: Habit 3: Put First Things First
chapters.summary: Habit 3 is the 'second creation' — executing your priorities. Covey's time matrix sorts activities by urgency and importance. Effective people spend more time in Quadrant II — important but not urgent: planning, relationships, prevention, learning — and say no to unimportant demands. Plan weekly around roles and goals.
keyIdeas: Schedule priorities, don't prioritise the schedule.
chapters.tryThis: Block one hour this week for a Quadrant II activity.

quiz.question: Which quadrant should effective people focus on?
quiz.explanation: Quadrant II prevents crises and builds the future.

chapters.title: Paradigms of Interdependence
chapters.summary: Covey introduces the Emotional Bank Account: trust built through deposits like understanding others, keeping promises, attending to small kindnesses, clarifying expectations, showing integrity and apologising sincerely. Strong relationships rest on a high balance of trust.
keyIdeas: Relationships run on an Emotional Bank Account.
chapters.tryThis: Make one deliberate deposit in an important relationship today.

quiz.question: What does the Emotional Bank Account measure?
quiz.explanation: Deposits build trust; withdrawals erode it.

chapters.title: Habit 4: Think Win/Win
chapters.summary: Win/Win seeks mutual benefit rather than one side winning at the other's expense. It needs character (integrity, maturity, an abundance mentality), trusting relationships, clear agreements and supportive systems. If a fair deal isn't possible, 'Win/Win or No Deal' frees both sides to walk away.
chapters.tryThis: Before your next negotiation, write what a win looks like for the other side.

quiz.question: What mindset underpins Win/Win?
quiz.explanation: Believing there's enough for everyone enables mutual wins.

chapters.title: Habit 5: Seek First to Understand, Then to Be Understood
chapters.summary: Most people listen with intent to reply. Covey teaches empathic listening — listening to understand the other person's frame of reference, feelings and meaning — before presenting your own view. Diagnose before you prescribe, then express yourself clearly with credibility, empathy and logic.
keyIdeas: Listen to understand, not to reply.
chapters.tryThis: In your next conversation, summarise the other person's view before giving yours.

quiz.question: What is empathic listening?
options: Listening to understand the other's frame of reference

chapters.title: Habit 6: Synergize
chapters.summary: Synergy means the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. By valuing differences and communicating with high trust and cooperation, people can find third alternatives better than either original position. Synergy is the fruit of the earlier habits working together.
chapters.tryThis: In a disagreement, ask: 'Would you be willing to look for a solution better than both of ours?'

quiz.question: What is a 'third alternative'?
options: A new solution better than either original
quiz.explanation: Synergy creates options neither side saw alone.

chapters.title: Habit 7: Sharpen the Saw
chapters.summary: Like a woodcutter who stops to sharpen his saw, we must renew ourselves to stay effective. Covey describes four dimensions: physical (exercise, rest, nutrition), spiritual (values, reflection), mental (reading, learning) and social/emotional (relationships). Balanced renewal creates an upward spiral of growth.
keyIdeas: Four dimensions: physical, spiritual, mental, social/emotional.
chapters.tryThis: Plan one renewal activity in each of the four dimensions this week.

quiz.question: Which is NOT one of the four renewal dimensions?
quiz.explanation: The four are physical, spiritual, mental and social/emotional.

chapters.title: Inside-Out Again
chapters.summary: Covey closes by returning to the inside-out approach: we can become transition figures who stop unhealthy patterns passed down to us instead of passing them on. Principle-centred living, he argues, is a lifelong process of growth and of reconnecting with what matters.
chapters.tryThis: Name one pattern you inherited that you want to stop with you.

quiz.question: What is a 'transition person'?
options: Someone who stops unhealthy patterns from passing on
quiz.explanation: They break the chain for the next generation.
